title: Common ion effect and buffer solutions
competency: Explain the common-ion effect and buffer action, and calculate the pH of buffers with the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation.

keywords.def: The shift of an ionic equilibrium when an ion already in it is added.
A solution of a weak acid and its conjugate base (or a weak base and its conjugate acid) that resists pH change.
pKa = −log Ka. A smaller pKa means a stronger acid.

en.text: Adding an ion that is already part of an ionic equilibrium shifts it, by Le Chatelier's principle. Adding HCl (H₃O⁺) or sodium acetate (CH₃COO⁻) to acetic acid shifts CH₃COOH + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + CH₃COO⁻ to the left, so less acetic acid ionizes. This is the common-ion effect.

am.text: በሚዛን ውስጥ ያለ አዮን ሲጨመር ሚዛኑ ወደ ግራ ይሄዳል (የለ ሻትሊዬ መርህ)፤ ይህ የጋራ አዮን ውጤት ነው።

screens.title: Add HCl to vinegar
screens.ask: You add some HCl to acetic acid solution. What happens to the ionization of acetic acid?
opts: Acetic acid becomes a strong acid
screens.after: HCl adds H₃O⁺, a product of acetic acid ionization, so the equilibrium shifts left.

screens.title: Le Chatelier and the common ion
paras: Adding a product shifts an equilibrium to the left.
HCl supplies H₃O⁺; CH₃COONa supplies CH₃COO⁻.

screens.title: 0.10 M acetic acid with 0.10 M HCl
steps: HCl gives 0.10 M H₃O⁺. ICE: [CH₃COOH] = 0.10 − x, [CH₃COO⁻] = x, [H₃O⁺] = 0.10 + x.
Without HCl, [CH₃COO⁻] would be 1.3 × 10⁻³ M: about 75 times more.

screens.why: x = √(3.6 × 10⁻⁶) = 1.9 × 10⁻³ M; pH = 2.72. With 0.30 M acetate it rises to 4.92.

en.text: A buffer resists changes in pH when a little acid or base is added. It contains a weak acid and its conjugate base (or a weak base and its conjugate acid) in comparable, fairly large amounts. Added H⁺ is taken up by the base (CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺ → CH₃COOH); added OH⁻ by the acid (CH₃COOH + OH⁻ → CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O). Blood is buffered near pH 7.4.

am.text: ባፈር ትንሽ አሲድ ወይም ቤዝ ሲጨመር pHን አይለውጥም። ደካማ አሲድና ተጓዳኝ ቤዙን ይይዛል። ደም በpH 7.4 አካባቢ ይጠበቃል።

screens.title: Which keeps its pH?
screens.ask: Two 1.0 L solutions both have pH 4.8: very dilute HCl, and an acetic acid/sodium acetate mixture. 0.010 mol NaOH is added to each. Which keeps its pH?
screens.after: The HCl solution jumps to pH 12.0; the mixture stays near 4.8. The mixture is a buffer.

screens.title: What a buffer is
paras: A buffer resists pH change when a little acid or base is added.
It is a weak acid + its conjugate base, or a weak base + its conjugate acid.

screens.title: How it works
paras: Added base: CH₃COOH + OH⁻ → CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O.
Only the ratio of the two parts changes a little.
Buffers keep blood at pH 7.4; gastric juice is about 1.5.

screens.title: Key word
defs: A solution of a weak acid and its conjugate base (or a weak base and its conjugate acid) that resists pH change.

screens.why: A buffer needs a weak acid/base and its conjugate. HCl and NaOH are strong.
screens.clue: Look for a WEAK acid or base with its conjugate.

screens.text: A little HCl is added to an acetic acid/acetate buffer. Which buffer part reacts?
screens.why: The conjugate base takes up added H⁺: CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺ → CH₃COOH.

screens.text: A buffer has its greatest capacity when
opts: the acid is much larger than the base
screens.why: Equal amounts can absorb acid or base equally well. More concentrated buffers also resist more.

screens.ask: 100 mL of 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ M HCl (pH 4.74, unbuffered) gets 1.0 mL of 0.10 M NaOH. New pH ≈ ___ (1 decimal place)
screens.why: Excess OH⁻ = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ − 1.8 × 10⁻⁶ = 9.8 × 10⁻⁵ mol in 0.101 L: 9.7 × 10⁻⁴ M. pOH 3.01, pH 10.99. A buffer would barely move.
screens.clue: Find the excess OH⁻ in moles, then divide by the new volume.

en.text: From Ka = [H₃O⁺][A⁻]/[HA], taking −log gives pH = pKa + log([conjugate base]/[weak acid]). For a weak base buffer, pOH = pKb + log([conjugate acid]/[weak base]). When the two parts are equal, pH = pKa. Added strong acid or base first reacts with a buffer part, then the new ratio gives the pH.

am.text: pH = pKa + log([ተጓዳኝ ቤዝ]/[ደካማ አሲድ])። ሁለቱ እኩል ሲሆኑ pH = pKa።

screens.title: Mix a buffer
screens.ask: Acetic acid buffer (pKa = 4.74). Change the amounts of acid and acetate.

screens.title: Deriving the equation
paras: Take −log of both sides: pH = pKa − log([HA]/[A⁻]).
Weak base buffers: pOH = pKb + log([conjugate acid]/[weak base]).

screens.ask: 0.060 M NH₃ and 0.040 M NH₄Cl (Kb = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵). pH ≈ ___ (2 decimal places)
0.40 M CH₃COOH and 0.20 M CH₃COO⁻ (Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵). pH ≈ ___ (2 decimal places)
screens.clue: More acid than base: pH below pKa.

screens.ask: 1.0 mL of 0.10 M HCl is added to 100 mL of the 0.1 M/0.1 M acetate buffer. New pH ≈ ___ (2 decimal places)
screens.why: 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol H⁺: acetate 0.0099 mol, acid 0.0101 mol. pH = 4.745 + log(0.0099/0.0101) = 4.736 ≈ 4.74. It barely moves.
screens.clue: React the H⁺ with acetate first, then use the mole ratio.
